claims.text: A sparse set of short ab initio molecular-dynamics trajectories is sufficient to train an on-the-fly machine-learned potential for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The trained machine-learned potential can accurately reproduce the free-energy landscapes of both crystalline and molten high-entropy alloys.
The proposed potential can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling in the calculated free energies.
The nested two-step protocol would substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations.
Al–Cr–Co–Fe–Ni is a five-component high-entropy-alloy system suitable as a target for potential-based molecular-dynamics modeling.
The target states include both crystalline solid solutions and molten alloys near and above melting.
Thermodynamic integration or nested sampling on the machine-learned potential can generate complete free-energy curves for both phases.
The protocol is applicable from approximately ambient temperature to 200–300 K above the melting point.
The protocol is applicable to alloys containing up to five principal elements.
Calibration against high-fidelity first-principles data allows a fitted interatomic potential to retain first-principles-like accuracy.
A trained machine-learned potential permits efficient evaluation of the configurations needed for free-energy integration.
The proposed method should closely reproduce ab initio molecular-dynamics solid–liquid free-energy differences.
The method should closely reproduce derived melting observables, including melting temperature, latent heat, and entropy of fusion.
The proposed method should reduce computation time by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The proposed method should scale significantly better than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Performance for systems containing more than five components or under extreme nonequilibrium conditions has not been validated.
Sparse ab initio sampling may fail to capture all relevant anharmonic effects and electron–vibration coupling in complex multicomponent alloys.
